title: Connected talk
verifiedBy: Claude Fable 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: A turn is where pro-drop is most tempting to break. Once the person is established, Italian keeps dropping the subject pronoun — and an io at the head of every sentence reads as insistence or contrast, not as neutral speech. The ending carries the person; a pronoun MARKS something.

lui and lei are for PEOPLE, and they earn their place only where a turn switches person or draws a contrast: Anna è italiana: lei è di Roma. Rohan è indiano: lui è di Delhi. For a THING Italian reaches for no pronoun at all — it drops the subject and lets the verb and the agreeing adjective carry the gender.

e ("and") is M1's è ("is") with the accent taken off, and both turn up inside the same turns. Write è on every copula and e bare — Il caffè è buono e caldo — because one missing accent turns a sentence into a list.
The joiners that hold a turn together are the module's whole new spend: e, ma, anche, poi, allora. Everything else comes from M1–M9.

anche goes IN FRONT of what it adds to, not at the end of the sentence: Anche Anna vuole un caffè ("Anna wants one too"). English can hang "too" on the end; Italian puts anche beside the word it is about, and moving it moves the meaning.

Each item here is a TURN of two or three short sentences — a question and its answer, or a statement, a reason and a follow-up. The word bound applies to each sentence inside the turn, not to the turn.

sentences.display: Come stai? Sto bene, grazie. E tu?
sentences.cue: How are you? — I'm fine, thanks. And you?
sentences.glossEn: lit. "How you-are-doing? I-am-doing well, thanks. And you?"
sentences.literal: How you-are-doing? I-am-doing well, thanks. And you?

words.note: and — one bare letter, and it is M1's è with the accent taken off. è is the verb "is"; e joins two things. They are otherwise identical on the page, so the accent is the whole difference.
The subject pronoun for one person. It is not needed to say "you" — the verb ending does that — so writing it MARKS a contrast, which is exactly what E tu? is doing: turning the same question back.

sentences.trap: E tu? is the one place in this course where a subject pronoun is compulsory: there is no verb behind it for an ending to sit on, so the pronoun has to carry the whole question.
sentences.sound: E is a single close vowel, said quickly and leaning onto the word after it. TU is short — the u is the oo of "moon", cut off.

variations.display: Come stai? Sto molto bene. E tu?
variations.cue: How are you? — I'm very well. And you?
variations.changed: molto turns the answer up; the turn is otherwise the same

variations.display: Come stai? Non sto bene oggi.
variations.cue: How are you? — I'm not well today.
variations.changed: an honest answer, with non in front of the verb and no question back

variations.display: Ciao, Anna! Come stai?
variations.cue: Hi, Anna! How are you?
variations.changed: a greeting in front, and the turn cut to two sentences

mistake.display: Come stai? Io sto bene, grazie. E tu?
mistake.why: Drop the io — sto already says who. The pronoun is right in E tu?, where nothing else can carry it, and wrong in the answer, where the ending already has.

sentences.usage: The first thirty seconds of any conversation.
sentences.mnemonic: The pronoun comes back only where no ending can do its job.

sentences.display: Che cosa fai domani? Domani lavoro, ma di sera sono libero.
sentences.cue: What are you doing tomorrow? — Tomorrow I'm working, but in the evening I'm free.
sentences.glossEn: lit. "What thing you-do tomorrow? Tomorrow I-work, but of evening I-am free."
sentences.literal: What thing you-do tomorrow? Tomorrow I-work, but of-evening I-am free.

words.note: but. It joins two whole sentences and always stands between them, exactly as in English.
free, in the sense of having no plans — and it agrees like any -o adjective: libero for a man, libera for a woman.

sentences.trap: Neither half of this answer has a subject word, and neither needs one: lavoro and sono each name their own person. Adding io to the second half would say "I, unlike you, am free".
sentences.sound: MA is one open syllable. LI-be-ro is stressed on the first of three, which is why it is not written with an accent.

variations.display: Che cosa fai domani? Domani non lavoro.
variations.cue: What are you doing tomorrow? — Tomorrow I'm not working.
variations.changed: one clause instead of two, with non in front of the verb

variations.display: Che cosa fai stasera? Stasera sono libera.
variations.cue: What are you doing tonight? — Tonight I'm free.
variations.changed: a woman answering, so the adjective goes to -a

variations.display: Domani lavoro, ma la settimana prossima sono libero.
variations.cue: Tomorrow I'm working, but next week I'm free.
variations.changed: a longer time phrase in the second half, joined by the same ma

mistake.display: Che cosa fai domani? Io domani lavoro, ma io di sera sono libero.
mistake.why: Two pronouns too many. Once the person is established, Italian keeps dropping it — Domani lavoro, ma di sera sono libero.

sentences.usage: Making a plan across two people's diaries.
sentences.mnemonic: ma joins two sentences; it never starts one on its own here.

sentences.display: Voglio un caffè. Anche Anna vuole un caffè.
sentences.cue: I want a coffee. Anna wants one too.
sentences.glossEn: lit. "I-want a coffee. Also Anna wants a coffee."
sentences.literal: I-want a coffee. Also Anna wants a coffee.

words.note: "Also", and it goes IN FRONT of whatever it adds to: Anche Anna vuole un caffè says Anna wants one as well as me; Anna vuole anche un caffè would say she wants a coffee as well as something else. Moving it moves the meaning.

sentences.trap: English hangs "too" on the end of the sentence and lets the stress decide what it applies to. Italian cannot: anche has to stand beside the word it is about, and where it stands is the meaning.
sentences.sound: AN-ke. The che is KE — a c before h is always hard.

variations.display: Voglio un caffè. Anche io voglio una pizza.
variations.cue: I want a coffee. I want a pizza too.
variations.changed: anche in front of a pronoun — one of the few places io belongs

variations.display: Voglio un caffè. Anna vuole anche una pizza.
variations.cue: I want a coffee. Anna wants a pizza as well.
variations.changed: anche moved in front of the pizza, so it is the pizza that is extra

variations.display: Anche Rohan vuole un caffè.
variations.cue: Rohan wants a coffee too.
variations.changed: one sentence on its own — anche is still in front of the person

mistake.display: Voglio un caffè. Anna vuole un caffè anche.
mistake.why: anche does not go on the end. In front of the person it adds: Anche Anna vuole un caffè.

sentences.usage: Ordering for two, and agreeing with someone.
sentences.mnemonic: anche leans on the word behind it, so put it where you mean it.

sentences.display: Ho fame. Allora vado a mangiare.
sentences.cue: I'm hungry. Well then, I'm off to eat.
sentences.glossEn: lit. "I-have hunger. Then I-go to eat."
sentences.literal: I-have hunger. Then I-go to eat.

words.note: "Well then" — the word that turns a fact into a decision. It is looser than quindi: quindi states a consequence, allora announces what you are going to do about it. It also opens a sentence when you are gathering your thoughts.

sentences.trap: quindi and allora both come out as English "so", and they are not the same: quindi is a conclusion, allora is a decision. If you could put "therefore" there, it is quindi.
sentences.sound: al-LO-ra, with the double l held and a tapped r.

variations.display: Ho fame. Allora mangiamo una pizza.
variations.cue: I'm hungry. Well then, let's eat a pizza.
variations.changed: the -iamo ending turns it into "let's" — the shape a decision for two takes

variations.display: Ho fame, quindi vado a mangiare.
variations.cue: I'm hungry, so I'm going to eat.
variations.changed: one sentence instead of two, and quindi states it as a consequence

variations.display: Piove. Allora prendo il treno.
variations.cue: It's raining. Well then, I'll take the train.
variations.changed: another fact and another decision, on the same hinge

mistake.display: Ho fame allora vado a mangiare.
mistake.why: allora opens its own sentence, so it needs the full stop in front of it — or a comma at the very least. Ho fame. Allora vado a mangiare.

sentences.usage: The moment a conversation turns into a plan.

sentences.display: Ieri sono andato a Roma. Poi sono tornato a casa.
sentences.cue: Yesterday I went to Rome. Then I came back home.
sentences.glossEn: lit. "Yesterday I-am gone to Rome. Then I-am returned to home."
sentences.literal: Yesterday I-am gone to Rome. Then I-am returned to home.

words.note: then, in the sense of next. It opens the second sentence of a sequence and needs no comma behind it.
The participle of tornare, "to come back" — and tornare is on the essere list with andare, so the past is sono tornato and the ending agrees: tornata for a woman.

sentences.trap: Both halves take essere, so both participles agree with whoever is speaking. A woman writing this turn writes sono andata and sono tornata, and changing one without the other is the slip to watch for.
sentences.sound: POI is one syllable — the o and the i glide together. tor-NA-to is stressed in the middle.

variations.display: Ieri sono andata a Roma. Poi sono tornata a casa.
variations.cue: Yesterday I went to Rome. Then I came back home.
variations.changed: a woman's turn — BOTH participles move to -a together

variations.display: Ieri sono andato a Milano. Poi ho mangiato una pizza.
variations.cue: Yesterday I went to Milan. Then I ate a pizza.
variations.changed: the second half swaps to avere, so its participle stops agreeing

variations.display: Sono andato a Roma e poi a Milano.
variations.cue: I went to Rome and then to Milan.
variations.changed: one sentence instead of two, joined by e — and the verb is not repeated

mistake.display: Ieri sono andata a Roma. Poi sono tornato a casa.
mistake.why: One speaker, two endings: pick one. Sono andata … sono tornata, or sono andato … sono tornato.

sentences.usage: Telling someone what you did with a day.
sentences.mnemonic: One speaker, one ending, all the way through the turn.

sentences.display: Anna è italiana: lei è di Roma. Rohan è indiano: lui è di Delhi.
sentences.cue: Anna is Italian: she's from Rome. Rohan is Indian: he's from Delhi.
sentences.glossEn: lit. "Anna is Italian: she is of Rome. Rohan is Indian: he is of Delhi."
sentences.literal: Anna is Italian: she is of Rome. Rohan is Indian: he is of Delhi.

words.note: she — the subject pronoun for a woman. It is not needed to say "she": the ending of è already does. It earns its place here because the turn has TWO people in it and the sentence is switching between them. (Written with a capital L in the middle of a sentence, Lei is also the polite "you", which this course does not teach.)
he — the partner of lei, and used the same way: only where a turn switches person or draws a contrast. For a THING Italian reaches for no pronoun at all.

sentences.trap: Two people in one turn is the situation these pronouns exist for. With only one person in play, Italian drops them again: Anna è italiana. È di Roma.
sentences.sound: LEY and LU-i, each one syllable and a half. lei is sei without its s; lui rhymes with it.

variations.display: Anna è italiana. È di Roma.
variations.cue: Anna is Italian. She's from Rome.
variations.changed: one person only, so no pronoun at all — the ending is enough

variations.display: Anna è di Roma, ma lavora a Milano.
variations.cue: Anna is from Rome, but she works in Milan.
variations.changed: one sentence instead of two, and still only one mention of her

variations.display: Rohan è indiano. Lui è di Delhi.
variations.cue: Rohan is Indian. He's from Delhi.
variations.changed: half the turn on its own — lui opens the second sentence about him

mistake.display: Anna è italiana: lei è di Roma, ma lei lavora a Milano.
mistake.why: The second lei is one too many. The verb ending already says who, and repeating the pronoun reads as a contrast that is not there.

sentences.usage: Introducing someone who is not in the room.
sentences.mnemonic: Name her once, then let the endings carry her.

sentences.display: Il caffè è buono e caldo. Ma è caro.
sentences.cue: The coffee is good and hot. But it's expensive.
sentences.glossEn: lit. "The coffee is good and hot. But is expensive."
sentences.literal: The coffee is good and hot. But is expensive.

words.note: expensive — and, of a person, dear. It agrees like any -o adjective: un caffè caro, una pizza cara.

sentences.trap: For a THING Italian writes no pronoun at all — not "it". The second sentence simply starts with the verb: È di Roma. esso exists and nobody says it.
sentences.sound: The two little words are heard apart as well as written apart: è is open, like the e of "bed"; e is close, nearer the a of "gate" without the glide.

variations.display: La pizza è buona e calda.
variations.cue: The pizza is good and hot.
variations.changed: a feminine subject pulls BOTH adjectives with it

variations.display: Il caffè è buono, ma è freddo.
variations.cue: The coffee is good, but it's cold.
variations.changed: ma joining inside one sentence, with the verb repeated because the clause is new

variations.display: Il caffè e la pizza sono buoni.
variations.cue: The coffee and the pizza are good.
variations.changed: e joining two SUBJECTS, so the verb goes plural

mistake.display: Il caffè e buono e caldo.
mistake.why: The first e should be è. Without its accent the sentence has no verb at all — it is a list of three things.

sentences.usage: Saying what you think of what is in front of you.
sentences.mnemonic: One accent is the difference between a sentence and a list.

sentences.display: Un caffè, per favore. Grazie. Prego.
sentences.cue: A coffee, please. — Thank you. — You're welcome.
sentences.glossEn: lit. "A coffee, please. Thanks. You're welcome."

words.note: The answer to grazie — and it does more than one job: it is also "after you", "go ahead", and what a shopkeeper says to invite your order. Whenever an English speaker would say "please" out of politeness rather than to ask, Italian is often saying prego.

sentences.trap: prego is not "please" — that is per favore. It is what comes AFTER a thank you, or what invites you to speak.
sentences.sound: PRE-go, with a close e and a hard g.

variations.display: Due caffè, per favore. Grazie.
variations.cue: Two coffees, please. — Thank you.
variations.changed: a number instead of an article; caffè does not go plural

variations.display: Vorrei un caffè, per favore.
variations.cue: I'd like a coffee, please.
variations.changed: the polite verb in front, for a counter where a bare noun feels blunt

variations.display: Grazie mille. Prego.
variations.cue: Thanks a lot. — You're welcome.
variations.changed: mille turns the thanks up — literally "a thousand thanks"

mistake.why: prego is not "please": asking for something takes per favore. Un caffè, per favore.

sentences.usage: The whole transaction at an Italian bar, in three words each.

sentences.display: Che cosa fai stasera? Vado al cinema con Anna.
sentences.cue: What are you doing tonight? — I'm going to the cinema with Anna.
sentences.glossEn: lit. "What thing you-do this-evening? I-go to-the cinema with Anna."
sentences.literal: What thing you-do this-evening? I-go to-the cinema with Anna.

words.note: Masculine, despite the -a: il cinema, al cinema. It is one of the counter-examples to "-a is feminine" — with il problema and il programma — and it never changes shape in the plural either.

sentences.trap: cinema ends in -a and is masculine, which is why the article is il and the fusion is al. The ending is a hint and never a rule.
sentences.sound: CHI-ne-ma, stressed on the FIRST of three syllables, and the c before i is soft.

variations.display: Che cosa fai stasera? Vado al bar con Rohan.
variations.cue: What are you doing tonight? — I'm going to the bar with Rohan.
variations.changed: another place with the same fused article, and another person

variations.display: Che cosa fai stasera? Non esco.
variations.cue: What are you doing tonight? — I'm not going out.
variations.changed: a refusal instead of a plan, in one short verb

variations.display: Stasera vado al cinema. Poi vado a casa.
variations.cue: Tonight I'm going to the cinema. Then I'm going home.
variations.changed: two halves of a plan, sequenced with poi

mistake.why: cinema is masculine, so the fusion is al: vado al cinema.

sentences.usage: The evening plan, asked and answered.
sentences.mnemonic: il cinema, il problema, il programma — three -a words that are masculine.

sentences.display: Buongiorno! Vorrei un chilo di pane, per favore. Grazie mille.
sentences.cue: Good morning! I'd like a kilo of bread, please. Thanks very much.
sentences.glossEn: lit. "Good day! I-would-like a kilo of bread, please. Thanks thousand."
sentences.literal: Good day! I-would-like a kilo of bread, please. Thanks thousand.

words.note: a thousand — and grazie mille is literally "a thousand thanks", the everyday way to turn a thank you up. It is the one number in this course that turns up outside a price.

sentences.trap: This whole turn is the register decision in three sentences: it is a stranger behind a counter, and there is not a single second-person verb in it. per favore and vorrei carry the politeness, so the tu / Lei question never has to be answered.
sentences.sound: MIL-le, with the double l genuinely held. grazie mille runs together as GRA-tsye-MIL-le.

variations.display: Buongiorno! Vorrei due bottiglie di vino, per favore.
variations.cue: Good morning! I'd like two bottles of wine, please.
variations.changed: a counted container instead of a weight — the frame is the same

variations.display: Buongiorno! Quanto costa un chilo di pane?
variations.cue: Good morning! How much does a kilo of bread cost?
variations.changed: the price question instead of the order, and still no second person

variations.display: Vorrei un chilo di pane. Grazie mille. Arrivederci.
variations.cue: I'd like a kilo of bread. Thanks very much. Goodbye.
variations.changed: the whole transaction, closed with the neutral goodbye

mistake.display: Buongiorno! Voglio un chilo di pane. Grazie mille.
mistake.why: Not wrong, but blunt across a counter: vorrei is what softens it. Vorrei un chilo di pane, per favore.

sentences.usage: A bakery, a market stall, or any counter with a queue behind you.
sentences.mnemonic: vorrei and per favore do the politeness this course's tu cannot.

comprehensionPool.cue: How are you? — I'm very well, thanks.

comprehensionPool.display: Che cosa fai domani? Vado a Roma con Anna.

comprehensionPool.display: Voglio una pizza. Anche Rohan vuole una pizza.
comprehensionPool.cue: I want a pizza. Rohan wants one too.

comprehensionPool.display: Ho sete. Allora bevo un po' di acqua.
comprehensionPool.cue: I'm thirsty. Well then, I'll drink a bit of water.

comprehensionPool.display: Ieri sono andata a Milano. Poi sono tornata a casa.
comprehensionPool.cue: Yesterday I went to Milan. Then I came back home.

comprehensionPool.display: Anna è italiana. Lei lavora a Milano.
comprehensionPool.cue: Anna is Italian. She works in Milan.

comprehensionPool.display: La pizza è buona e calda.
comprehensionPool.cue: The pizza is good and hot.

comprehensionPool.display: Stasera vado al cinema. Poi vado a casa.

comprehensionPool.cue: I'm not going out tonight because I'm sleepy.

comprehensionPool.cue: Anna works in Milan, but she's from Rome.
